title: TOTP: Time-Based One-Time Password Algorithm
subtitle: How an authenticator app and a server agree on a six-digit code without talking to each other.
summary: TOTP extends the HMAC-based one-time password (HOTP) algorithm of RFC 4226 by replacing its event counter with a value derived from the current time. The prover and the verifier share a secret key and count 30-second time steps from the Unix epoch, so both compute the same short code independently. It is the scheme behind most authenticator apps. The RFC is Informational, not a Standards Track document.

eli5.summary: You and a friend share a secret recipe and both look at the same clock. Every half minute you each cook up the same new password from the recipe and the time, so you never have to tell each other what it is.

tldr.problem: A server wants to check a user's second factor, but a static password can be stolen and replayed, and an event counter can fall out of step.
tldr.mechanism: Both sides compute HOTP(K, T), where T is the number of 30-second steps since the Unix epoch, and the verifier accepts the code only for the current step and a small allowed window.
tldr.outcome: Codes are short-lived, need no network round trip to generate, and work across vendors, which is why authenticator apps everywhere use it.

today:
TOTP is the code behind most authenticator apps and many hardware tokens. When a site asks for a six-digit code that refreshes about every 30 seconds, it is almost always computing the algorithm in this RFC. The RFC's own test vectors use eight digits; apps commonly show six, which is a matter of how many digits are kept from the same computation.

Because the code is a function of a shared secret and the clock, TOTP still needs a secure enrolment step to hand over the secret, and it does not stop a user from typing a live code into a phishing page.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 6238 describes an extension of the One-Time Password (OTP) algorithm, specifically the HMAC-based One-Time Password (HOTP) algorithm defined in RFC 4226, so that it supports a time-based moving factor. HOTP takes a shared secret K and an increasing counter C and truncates an HMAC-SHA-1 result into a user-friendly number. TOTP is the time-based variant: a value T, derived from a time reference and a time step, takes the place of the counter C.

The RFC also lets implementations use HMAC-SHA-256 or HMAC-SHA-512 instead of the HMAC-SHA-1 that HOTP specifies.

RFC 6238 is Informational. It was published in May 2011 "for informational purposes" rather than as a Standards Track specification, although it became the de facto standard for authenticator apps.
sections.eli5: A counting game needs both players to keep the same count. If one of you misses a round, you are out of sync. TOTP counts with the clock instead, and the clock keeps everyone in step.

sections.title: Algorithm Requirements
sections.content:
Section 3 lists seven requirements, R1 to R7, that shaped the design. The prover (a token or soft token) and the verifier (the authentication or validation server) must each know or be able to derive the current Unix time. They must share a secret, or know a secret transformation that produces one. The algorithm must use HOTP as a building block, and both sides must use the same time-step value X.

Each prover must have a unique key. Keys should be randomly generated or derived with a key derivation algorithm, and may be stored in a tamper-resistant device, but should always be protected against unauthorized access.
sections.eli5: For the trick to work, you both need the same secret, the same clock and the same rule for how often the code changes. Everyone also gets their own secret, so one stolen secret does not open every door.

sections.title: The TOTP Algorithm
sections.content:
Two system parameters drive the calculation. X is the time step in seconds, with a default of 30. T0 is the Unix time at which counting starts, with a default of 0, the Unix epoch. TOTP is defined as TOTP = HOTP(K, T), where T = (Current Unix time - T0) / X, using the floor function. With T0 = 0 and X = 30, T is 1 at Unix time 59 seconds and 2 at 60 seconds.

HOTP then runs HMAC over the 8-byte value of T with the key K and truncates the result to the requested number of digits. The reference code reads the low four bits of the last byte of the hash as an offset, takes four bytes from there with the top bit cleared, and reduces the result modulo a power of ten.

Implementations must support a value of T larger than a 32-bit integer so that they keep working beyond the year 2038. The values of X and T0 are agreed during provisioning, which the RFC leaves out of scope and points to RFC 6030 for a container format.
sections.eli5: Divide the number of seconds since 1970 by 30 and throw away the leftover. Mix that number with your secret, squash the result down to a few digits, and that is your code. Everyone who knows the secret gets the same digits.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The strength of TOTP depends on HOTP, which is built on HMAC with SHA-1. The analysis in RFC 4226 concludes that, for practical purposes, the outputs of dynamic truncation on distinct inputs are uniformly and independently distributed strings, and that the best attack against the HOTP function is brute force.

Keys should be chosen at random, or by a cryptographically strong pseudorandom generator properly seeded, following RFC 4086. They should be the length of the HMAC output to help interoperability. All communications should take place over a secure channel such as TLS (RFC 5246) or IPsec (RFC 4301).

On the validation side the RFC recommends storing keys encrypted in tamper-resistant hardware and decrypting them only when needed, then re-encrypting at once to limit exposure in RAM. The key store must be in a secure area, and access limited to the programs the validation system needs.
sections.eli5: The whole trick is only as safe as the secret. If a thief learns it, they can make the same codes you do, so the checker has to keep every secret locked away.

sections.title: Validation and Time-Step Size
sections.content:
An OTP generated within one time step is the same for the whole step. The verifier does not know exactly when the user generated a code, so it typically uses the time it received the code. Network delay can push a code generated at the end of one step into the next, so the verifier should accept earlier steps too, within a policy window. The RFC recommends allowing at most one time step for network delay.

Step size is a trade-off. A larger step gives an attacker who sees a code more time to use it, and also makes an honest user wait longer for the next code. The RFC recommends a default of 30 seconds as a balance between security and usability, and notes that a window as large as 10 minutes would hardly suit typical login use.

The verifier must not accept a second attempt of the same OTP after one successful validation. This is what makes the password one-time within its step.
sections.eli5: A code lasts about half a minute. The checker is a little forgiving in case your code was slow to arrive, but once it has accepted a code it will never accept that same code again.

sections.title: Resynchronization
sections.content:
Prover and verifier clocks drift apart. The RFC recommends that the validator be set with a specific limit on the number of time steps a prover may be out of sync before being rejected, and that the limit can apply both forward and backward from the calculated step.

The worked example: with 30-second steps and a validator that accepts two steps backward, the maximum elapsed time drift is around 89 seconds, which is 29 seconds in the calculated time step plus 60 seconds for the two backward steps. The validator would check the current step and then two earlier ones, three validations in all.

After a successful validation the server can record the detected drift for that token, as a number of time steps, and apply it to later codes. If a prover has been silent for a long time, the accumulated drift may exceed the threshold. Then additional authentication measures should be used to authenticate the prover and explicitly resynchronize the clocks.
sections.eli5: Two watches never keep perfect time. The checker looks at one or two moments just before now as well, and remembers how far off your watch usually is. If your watch is way off, you have to prove who you are another way and set it right.

sections.title: Reference Code and Test Vectors
sections.content:
Appendix A gives a Java reference implementation, and Appendix B gives test values for interoperability. The test token's shared secret is the ASCII string "12345678901234567890", with X = 30 and T0 = 0, and the codes shown are eight digits long. Appendix A uses a 20-byte seed for SHA-1, a 32-byte seed for SHA-256 and a 64-byte seed for SHA-512, built by repeating that string.

The first row in the table below is the easiest to check by hand: at Unix time 59, T is 1, and the SHA-1 code is 94287082. Check your own implementation against all of them before trusting it.
sections.eli5: Before you trust your code maker, you ask it a few questions whose answers are already published. If it gets all of them right, it is working like everyone else's.

items.title: The time
items.text: Both sides know or derive the current Unix time (R1).

items.title: The secret
items.text: A unique key per prover, shared or derivable (R2, R5).

items.title: The step
items.text: The same time-step value X on both sides (R4).

items.title: The building block
items.text: HOTP, from RFC 4226, computes the code (R3).
